metaTitle: Water Bug vs Cockroach: How to Tell Them Apart
metaDescription: Water bug can mean a pond insect, the toe-biter, with a painful bite, or the cockroach in your basement. Photos and how to tell them apart.
h1: Water Bugs vs Cockroaches: How to Tell Which One You Found
dek: Why two unrelated insects share one nickname, how to tell a giant water bug from an Oriental or American cockroach by sight, and what each one means for your home.
excerpt: Two unrelated insects share the name water bug. Here is how to tell a biting giant water bug from an Oriental or American cockroach, and what to do about each.

quickAnswer.lead: **Water bug is a name for two different insects: the giant water bug, a pond insect nicknamed the toe-biter for its painful bite, and the cockroach in a basement or drain, usually an Oriental cockroach.** The giant water bug is brown, flat and up to about 2.5 inches long, with grasping front legs. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/oriental-cockroaches) says Oriental cockroaches earn the nickname from the dark, damp places they hide.
bullets: Giant water bugs are about 2 to 2.5 inches long, live in ponds, lakes and slow streams, and fly to lights on summer nights.
Oriental cockroaches are about 1 to 1.25 inches long, dark brown to nearly black, and do not fly.
American cockroaches are about 2 inches long and reddish brown, and both adult males and females can fly.
Mississippi State Extension describes a giant water bug bite as extremely painful but short-lived, with no long-term adverse effects.
Oriental cockroaches die within two weeks without water, so leaks and damp spots are the weak point.
Giant water bugs are not household pests, while Oriental and American cockroaches are.

facts.caption: The giant water bug is the true water bug; the cockroaches share the nickname. From Missouri's Department of Conservation, Mississippi State, Kentucky, Minnesota, UC IPM, Penn State and Texas A&M, all linked on this page. Sources differ slightly on sizes.

body.text: Are water bugs and cockroaches the same insect?

No. Water bug is a nickname that has landed on two unrelated insects: the giant water bug, which lives in ponds and bites, and the Oriental cockroach, which hides in damp basements and drains. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/oriental-cockroaches) says Oriental cockroaches are often called water bugs because they favor dark, damp, cool places such as under sinks and washing machines, and the [University of California's cockroach guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/) notes that the same species is sometimes called a water bug or a black beetle.

body.alt: Brown American giant water bug on sunlit red brick paving, seen from above, with a flat oval body and two hooked grasping front legs
body.caption: An American giant water bug on brick paving in Maryland. The person who photographed it reports a very painful bite after trying to move it by hand.

body.text: The name fits the giant water bug better. [Missouri's Department of Conservation](https://www.mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/giant-water-bugs) describes a brownish, flattened, beetle-like insect that lives in ponds and sluggish water and eats insects, crayfish, frogs, fish and young turtles and snakes. The [University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CritterFiles/casefile/insects/bugs/giantwater/giantwater.htm) records the confusion running the other way, listing water roach among the giant water bug's other names.

The two call for opposite responses. A giant water bug is a pond animal that strayed toward a light and is best left alone, while a roach in the house is a pest that needs a plan. If you want the background on the species behind the nickname first, [the complete cockroach guide for US homes](/learn/cockroaches) covers all of them.
How can you tell a giant water bug from a cockroach?

Start with the front legs and the head. The [University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CritterFiles/casefile/insects/bugs/giantwater/giantwater.htm) describes giant water bugs with large, prey-grasping front legs and a sharp piercing beak, and Missouri adds long, oar-like hind legs built for swimming. [UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/) describes cockroaches as broad, flattened insects with long antennae and a shield-shaped plate behind the head. Grasping front legs mean a water bug; long antennae and that shield-shaped plate mean a cockroach.

Sources differ slightly: about 2 versus up to 2.5 inches for the water bug, and about 1 versus 1.25 inches for the Oriental cockroach.

Top-down photo of an adult Oriental cockroach and an adult American cockroach side by side next to a US penny, showing the size and color difference, the shield-shaped plate behind the head and the long antennae

body.text: Behavior is a second clue. UC IPM describes cockroaches as mostly nocturnal insects that crawl quickly and may climb rough surfaces, and Penn State calls the Oriental cockroach sluggish, found at or below ground level and rarely on walls or upper floors. A large insect beside a lit doorway or floating in a swimming pool is more likely to be the aquatic one, as the next section explains.

If your insect matches neither column, compare it with [the beetles, crickets and wood roaches most often mistaken for a pest cockroach](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-cockroaches). A far smaller roach is probably another species, such as the one in [the German cockroach guide](/blog/german-cockroaches), and a small wingless insect may be a young roach, which [a photo guide to baby cockroaches by species](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) helps you check.
What is a giant water bug, and why is one at my door?

A giant water bug is a large aquatic predator that sometimes leaves the water on summer nights and flies toward bright lights. [Mississippi State University Extension](https://extension.msstate.edu/newsletters/bugs-eye-view/2024/giant-water-bug-vol-10-no-08) says adults reach up to 2.5 inches, live in ponds, lakes and streams throughout the country, and are relatively common but rarely seen. On summer nights they sometimes crawl out of the water and fly, it adds, and they are attracted to artificial lights, sometimes crash-landing nearby. Missouri says these night flights occasionally end with a bug in a swimming pool.

body.alt: Dark brown giant water bug on a light concrete sidewalk beside a crack, seen from above, with its grasping front legs held forward
body.caption: Uhler's giant water bug on the sidewalk outside a store in North Carolina. Look for the flat, oval body and the grasping front legs.
body.credit: (c) Matthew Lumsden, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: In the water, it is an ambush hunter. Mississippi State reports that young nymphs eat other insects and small aquatic invertebrates, while large nymphs and adults take minnows, tadpoles, frogs, and small snakes and turtles. The bug grabs prey with its front legs and injects saliva that paralyzes the victim and begins digesting it. Missouri calls giant water bugs generally beneficial because they consume mosquito larvae.

One oddity helps with identification. Missouri reports that the female lays her eggs in a flat cluster on the male's back, and that an egg-laden male cannot fly or mate until the eggs hatch. Kentucky adds that only some species do this. A water bug carrying a mat of eggs is therefore a male that is not about to fly to your porch light.

body.needed: Close-up photo of a male giant water bug with a flat cluster of eggs on its back, resting on a white surface or a gloved hand so the size is clear

body.text: What is a toe-biter?

Toe-biter is another name for the giant water bug, and it comes from the bite. [Missouri's Department of Conservation](https://www.mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/giant-water-bugs) says giant water bugs that are handled, or bothered by barefoot waders, can deliver an excruciatingly painful bite, hence the name. The [University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CritterFiles/casefile/insects/bugs/giantwater/giantwater.htm) lists toe-biters, belostomatids, water roaches and electric light bugs among its other names, and [the University of Minnesota's Department of Entomology](https://entomology.umn.edu/giant-water-bug) adds alligator ticks, for the insect's tick-like look.

The name covers several species. [Mississippi State University Extension](https://extension.msstate.edu/newsletters/bugs-eye-view/2024/giant-water-bug-vol-10-no-08) names two of the more common ones: *Benacus griseus*, colloquially called the eastern toe-biter, and *Lethocerus americanus*, the one officially known as the giant water bug. Not all of them are giants. Kentucky says its most commonly encountered giant water bugs are only about 1 inch long, and that its common *Belostoma* species look very similar to the big *Lethocerus* water bugs apart from their size.

body.alt: Large dark brown giant water bug lying across the fingers of an open hand, seen from above, with its grasping front legs folded
body.caption: A giant water bug of the species Mississippi State calls the eastern toe-biter, found in a parking garage in Louisiana and shown on an open hand for size.
body.credit: (c) Amber M. King, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Electric light bug comes from the night flights. The [University of Florida's giant water bug profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN578) says adults fly from pond to pond or pool of water in the mating season, and that during these flights they fly to lights in large numbers. Mississippi State says they leave the water on summer nights in search of mates, or to escape water that is drying up, and sometimes crash-land and end up stranded near lights. [University of Minnesota Extension](https://apps.extension.umn.edu/garden/diagnose/insect/general-curiosity-insects/beetles/large/giant-water-bug.html) finds them in shallow ponds and lakes from May to August, and around lights in yards, parking lots and recreational fields.

For all the name, the bite is a defense. UMN Extension says a mishandled giant water bug can jab you to defend itself, and Minnesota's entomologists point out that human toes are not on its menu. Florida adds that it can pinch with its front legs as well as bite with its strong beak. The section on water bug bites below covers how much it hurts; the practical rule is Kentucky's: giant water bugs can bite, so they should not be handled.
Why does the male carry eggs on its back?

Because in two groups of giant water bugs, *Abedus* and *Belostoma*, that is where the female lays them. The [University of Florida](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN578) says females of these two genera glue their eggs onto the males' backs, calls egg carrying by males a unique feature of the pair, and says the eggs hatch in one to two weeks. Missouri describes the result as a big, flat cluster that stays on the male until the young hatch.

Missouri's explanation is protection: on the male's back, the eggs are safe from the many aquatic animals that would otherwise eat them. The cost falls on the male, which Missouri says cannot fly or mate again until the eggs hatch, while the female often mates again. Florida even notes a report of females laying eggs on other females' backs when large enough males were scarce.

The big *Lethocerus* water bugs work differently. Florida says *Lethocerus* eggs are laid above the water on plants and other objects, and Minnesota's entomologists say the male American giant water bug guards them there. A giant water bug with a mat of eggs on its back is therefore usually an *Abedus* or *Belostoma* male, not a *Lethocerus*.
Which cockroaches do people call water bugs?

Mostly the Oriental cockroach, a dark, slow insect of damp, low places that does not fly. UC IPM lists it at about 1.25 inches and almost black, living in cool, dark, damp places such as garages, basements, water meter boxes and drains, and unable to climb smooth vertical surfaces. Penn State puts adults at about an inch, very dark brown to nearly black with a greasy sheen. The two sources differ by a fraction of an inch, so expect something between 1 and 1.25 inches.

body.alt: Shiny, nearly black Oriental cockroach on a gray concrete floor beside a dry leaf, seen from above
body.caption: An adult Oriental cockroach on a concrete garage floor in Pennsylvania. Look for the very dark, nearly black body Penn State describes.
body.credit: (c) Nelson Chu Pavlosky, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Males have short wings that cover about three-quarters of the abdomen, and females have only small, functionless wing pads, and UC IPM says the species does not fly. Penn State places the species indoors under porches, in drains, sewers, crawl spaces and damp basements, and gathered around leaks. Outdoors it lives in leaf litter, bark mulch around foundations, water valve pits and garbage areas, and it may move inside during dry spells to find humidity.

body.alt: Dozens of shiny black Oriental cockroaches in the grass at night around a rusty sewer manhole cover
body.caption: Oriental cockroaches out at night around a sewer manhole cover in Washington, DC, which the photographer saw them coming out of.
body.credit: (c) Carrie Seltzer, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: The [guide to the Oriental cockroach](/blog/oriental-cockroaches) shows males and females in photos and covers where the species lives, when it is most active and the checks that separate it from American, smokybrown and Turkestan cockroaches.
What about the American cockroach?

The American cockroach is the larger, reddish brown species that shares the Oriental cockroach's damp territory. UC IPM lists it at about 2 inches with light-colored edges on the plate behind the head, and Texas A&M AgriLife says both adult males and females can fly. It prefers warm, humid conditions, usually above 82°F (28°C), in places such as sewers, water meter boxes, storm drains and steam tunnels, and UC IPM says it readily lives outdoors under the right conditions. That overlap in size and in warm-evening flights is why a large flying insect at night can be either one. Which cockroaches really fly, and how well, is laid out in [the species-by-species guide to flying roaches](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly).

[Texas A&M AgriLife Extension](https://mytexas.ag.tamu.edu/publications/cockroach-biology-and-management/) lists waterbug and palmetto bug as other names for the American cockroach, puts adults at 1 1/2 to 2 inches, and says both males and females can fly. It also says American and Oriental cockroaches commonly enter buildings through floor drains, and advises keeping drain traps filled with water as a barrier between the sewer and the home.
The [palmetto bug guide](/blog/palmetto-bugs) compares the American cockroach with the other large roaches that go by that name, with photos.
Do water bugs bite?

Giant water bugs do, and the bite hurts; cockroach bites are a separate and much smaller question. Missouri says a giant water bug that is handled or disturbed by waders delivers an extremely painful bite, which is where the nickname toe-biter comes from. Mississippi State also calls the bites extremely painful, but says the pain is relatively short-lived with no long-term adverse effects, and that bites are rare because people seldom meet the insects. The University of Kentucky says bites can be painful and that some people have medically serious reactions, though it calls this very rare.

For most people, then, the sources describe sharp but short-lived pain, and Kentucky's note means a serious reaction is very rare but not impossible. Contact a healthcare provider if pain or swelling keeps getting worse, if symptoms spread, or if you have ever reacted badly to an insect bite. For the cockroaches, [what is actually documented about cockroach bites](/blog/do-cockroaches-bite) separates rare bites from the more common health issues covered next.
Are water bugs or cockroaches dangerous?

A giant water bug is a painful nuisance, and the cockroaches carry the larger health risk. The [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/asthma/asthma-triggers-gain-control) says certain proteins in cockroach feces and saliva can cause allergic reactions or trigger asthma symptoms in some people, and that droppings or body parts of cockroaches can trigger asthma.

Penn State links Oriental cockroaches to gastroenteritis, dysentery and diarrhea through disease organisms carried on their legs and bodies. It also lists allergic reactions to their droppings and shed skins, including sneezing, watery eyes, nasal congestion and asthma. UC IPM says the American cockroach is capable of transmitting the bacteria *Salmonella* and *Shigella*, which cause food poisoning. The sources use cautious wording such as capable of and linked to, so read these as documented risks, not as a certainty that any one roach has made someone sick.

If anyone in the home has asthma or allergy symptoms that are worse indoors and you are finding cockroaches, tell their healthcare provider about the infestation. The giant water bug has no comparable household risk; Kentucky says giant water bugs are not considered pests.

body.text: What should you do about a giant water bug?

Leave it alone, or move it outside without touching it, because it is not a household pest and the bite is the only real risk. Missouri describes the painful bite coming when waders handle or disturb the insect, and Mississippi State says bites are rare because encounters are infrequent. A bug stranded on a porch can be nudged into a container with a piece of cardboard and released near water, and one in a pool can be lifted out with a net.

Because adults are drawn to artificial lights, a bright light near a pond or pool is the likely draw. The sources describe that attraction, but none tests a lighting change as a fix, so there is no evidence-based method to offer. What they do show is that the visits are seasonal: Mississippi State ties the flights to summer nights.
Why is there a water bug in my pool?

Most likely it flew in at night. Missouri says giant water bugs are strong fliers that are attracted to artificial lights after dark, and that they are sometimes found in swimming pools as a result of these night trips. Florida describes adults flying from pond to pond or pool of water in the mating season, and UMN Extension says they are found from May to August.

body.alt: Brown Belostoma toe-biter on damp gray concrete, seen from above, with a flat oval body and short grasping front legs
body.caption: A Belostoma toe-biter, one of the smaller giant water bugs, pulled alive out of a swimming pool filter on Long Island, New York.
body.credit: (c) David LaMagna, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Lift it out with the pool's skimmer net, as Missouri advises because of the painful bite, and let it go away from the pool. Do not pick it up: Kentucky says giant water bugs can bite and should not be handled, and Florida says they can also pinch with their front legs. Mississippi State notes that children are among the most common bite victims, so keep them out of the water until it is gone.
None of the sources cited here recommends an insecticide for a giant water bug in a pool; Missouri's advice is a net. Any pesticide may be used only where and how its label directs.
How do you get rid of the cockroaches called water bugs?

Cut off water, close the gaps, and put bait where the roaches live. That is the pattern in the extension guidance, and it targets what these species need most: Penn State reports that Oriental cockroaches die within two weeks without water, although they can live a month without food when water is available.

items: **Dry out and clean up.** Penn State calls removing food, moisture and the harborages roaches shelter in the first step in treatment. The EPA's asthma guidance adds keeping counters, sinks, tables and floors clean and free of clutter, cleaning dishes, crumbs and spills right away, and storing food in airtight containers.

**Seal the entry routes.** UC IPM recommends sealing cracks and other openings and fitting door sweeps and weather stripping on doors and windows. It notes that American cockroaches foraging from sewers reach ground floors especially where pipes are damaged, screens are missing or drain water traps are faulty, so those are worth checking too. Penn State adds caulking in closets and cabinets and under the sink, and [how cockroaches get into a home and how to close each route](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from) walks through the rest.

**Monitor with sticky traps.** Penn State suggests setting sticky traps against walls and in corners at several sites for a week to learn how widespread the problem is. A guide to [how glue traps and bait stations do different jobs](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada) explains what traps can and cannot do.

**Bait the places they live.** For outdoor-living roaches, UC IPM recommends placing baits in water meter boxes, drains or under concrete slabs. Penn State lists bait active ingredients such as hydramethylnon, fipronil, boric acid and abamectin, placed where roaches harbor, and [why bait beats spray for cockroaches](/blog/best-cockroach-killer-canada) explains the reasoning.

body.title: Read the label first
body.text: Baits, dusts and sprays are pesticides. Use a product only where and how its label directs, and keep it away from children, pets and food. The EPA cautions that insecticides can harm people as well as pests and recommends choosing lower-risk methods.

Expect it to take time. UC IPM reports that Oriental cockroaches need 1 to 2 years or more to develop from nymph to adult, and that a female and her offspring can produce nearly 200 cockroaches in a year, so the population builds slowly but steadily while the damp conditions remain. A longer bait-first sequence is in [a step-by-step cockroach removal plan](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada).
When should you call a professional?

Call one if you keep finding cockroaches after the moisture is fixed and bait is down, if they seem to come from shared walls or sewer lines in a multi-unit building, or if someone in the home has asthma and the infestation is established. In an apartment, report the problem to the property manager as well.

A recurring problem at one drain may be a plumbing fault. UC IPM links cockroach entry from sewers to damaged pipes and faulty drain water traps, and those are repairs for a plumber, not something a pesticide can fix. A giant water bug at your door, by contrast, needs no professional at all.

faqs.question: Can giant water bugs fly?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mississippi State Extension says giant water bugs sometimes crawl out of the water on summer nights and fly, and that they are drawn to artificial lights. Missouri's Department of Conservation says these night flights occasionally land them in swimming pools. Among the cockroaches, Texas A&M AgriLife says both adult male and female American cockroaches can fly, while UC IPM says Oriental cockroaches do not fly. A large insect circling a light at night could therefore be either a giant water bug or an American cockroach, and the legs, size and color sort them out.

faqs.question: Is a giant water bug bite dangerous?
faqs.answer: Mississippi State Extension calls the bite extremely painful but says the pain is relatively short-lived and that there are no long-term adverse effects. The University of Kentucky says bites can be painful and that some people have medically serious reactions, though it calls this very rare. Contact a healthcare provider if the pain or swelling keeps getting worse, if symptoms spread, or if you have ever had an allergic reaction to an insect bite.

faqs.question: Why do I keep finding Oriental cockroaches in my basement?
faqs.answer: Oriental cockroaches seek cool, damp, dark places, and a basement with leaks, a floor drain or a crawl space offers all three. Penn State Extension says they enter in food packages and laundry and under doors, and may move indoors during dry spells to find humidity. Without water they die within two weeks, so repairing leaks and drying damp areas is the most useful step. Sealing cracks and placing bait where they live completes the job.

faqs.question: Can water bugs come up through drains?
faqs.answer: The cockroaches called water bugs can. UC IPM says Oriental cockroaches live in drains and water meter boxes, and that American cockroaches in sewers occasionally forage into ground-floor buildings, especially when pipes are damaged, screens are missing or drain water traps are faulty. The sources describe giant water bugs as living in ponds, slow streams and wetlands, not in plumbing. Sealing cracks and other openings is part of UC IPM's advice, and its mention of damaged pipes and faulty traps points to plumbing repairs as well.

faqs.question: Do giant water bugs eat mosquitoes?
faqs.answer: They eat the larvae. Missouri's Department of Conservation calls giant water bugs generally beneficial because they consume mosquito larvae. Larvae are only part of the diet, though: large nymphs and adults also eat minnows, tadpoles, frogs and small snakes and turtles, according to Mississippi State Extension. None of the sources reviewed here claims that the giant water bugs in a pond prevent a mosquito problem, so treat them as one natural predator among many and not as a control method.

faqs.question: What is a water bug?
faqs.answer: Water bug is a common name for two unrelated insects. The true water bug is the giant water bug, a brown, flat pond insect up to about 2.5 inches long with grasping front legs, also called the toe-biter and the electric light bug. In homes, the name usually means a cockroach: Penn State and UC IPM say the Oriental cockroach is called a water bug, and Texas A&M lists waterbug as another name for the American cockroach. The giant water bug is not a household pest; both cockroaches are.

faqs.question: Do water bugs bite?
faqs.answer: The giant water bug does, and the bite hurts. Missouri's Department of Conservation calls it excruciatingly painful, and Mississippi State Extension says people who have been bitten describe it as more painful than any other insect sting or bite they have had, though the pain is relatively short-lived with no long-term adverse effects. Bites are rare, and Missouri says they come when a bug is handled or disturbed by barefoot waders. The University of Kentucky notes that, very rarely, someone has a medically serious reaction. The cockroaches called water bugs are a different case: their main risks are allergens and germs.

faqs.question: Are water bugs and palmetto bugs the same thing?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, depending on who uses the names. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension lists waterbug and palmetto bug as other names for the American cockroach, a reddish brown roach about 2 inches long whose adults can fly. Penn State and UC IPM apply water bug to the Oriental cockroach, a smaller, nearly black roach that does not fly. Neither is the true water bug, the giant water bug of ponds and slow streams, which is not a cockroach and not a household pest.

faqs.question: Why do I have water bugs in my house?
faqs.answer: If the water bug is a cockroach, damp hiding places and easy ways in are the usual reasons. Penn State says Oriental cockroaches favor dark, damp, cool areas, gather around leaks in basements and crawl spaces, and may move indoors during dry spells in search of humidity. Texas A&M says American and Oriental cockroaches commonly come in through floor drains, and UC IPM says American cockroaches forage from sewers into ground floors where pipes are damaged or drain traps are faulty. A giant water bug near the house is more likely a stray drawn to lights at night.

faqs.question: What does a water bug look like?
faqs.answer: It depends on which one you mean. The giant water bug is brown, flat and oval, with large grasping front legs, a sharp, piercing beak and none of the long antennae a cockroach has. Mississippi State puts adults at up to 2.5 inches, though Kentucky says its most common kinds are only about 1 inch long. The Oriental cockroach called a water bug is about 1 to 1.25 inches long, dark brown to nearly black with a greasy sheen, and has short wings or only wing pads. Cockroaches have long antennae and a shield-shaped plate behind the head.
